There is a small, but defi- nite, risk that patients taking lithium in therapeutic doses will de- velop goitre, clinical or subclinical hypothyroidism, or, rarely, both.1-3 Published prevalence figures have varied widely al- though most studies have found an increased risk of hypothy- roidism in patients treated with lithium when compared to the general population.2 Prevalence also appears to be higher in women taking lithium than in men;2 in addition, the increased risk in women may be greatest during the first 2 years of lithium therapy. Other risk factors identified include a family history of thyroid disorders.3 However, a long-term, follow-up study4,5 suggested that the incidence of thyroid abnormalities was no greater in lithium-treated patients than in the general population. Early goitre and lithium-induced hypothyroidism are both re- versible if lithium is withdrawn; if continued treatment with lith- ium is desirable the patient should be treated with levothyroxine. There have been rare reports of hyperthyroidism in lithium-treat- ed patients6 and the association may only be one of coincidence, although it is important to realise that hyperthyroidism can pre- cipitate mania and can also be mistaken for an attack of mania. Increases in serum concentrations of calcium and parathyroid hormone have been described in patients receiving lithium ther- apy. Although generally considered to be slight, some patients have experienced parathyroid hyperplasia.7,8 Cases of diabetes mellitus developing in patients treated with lithium have been reported but may not be attributable to lithi- um.9 1.
